text.p: The following are the main stories from Tuesday morning's Austrian newspapers:
DER STANDARD

- Austria's government is undecided about when to start talks with Nato over the country's membership in the military alliance. Conservative state secretary in the Foreign Ministry Benita Ferrero-Waldner demands a speedy decision as a longer wait will cost more.
- The government will not appoint another representative for the introduction of Europe's single currency after the last person resigned.
- The agreement by the coalition parties and two of the three opposition parties over a reform of politicians' pay is threatened by the conservative state leaders' demands for higher pay.
- Die Erste savings bank and GiroCredit are likely to merge within the year. A first decision is expected by June 4. The regional savings bank wants to stop any further mergers between savings banks.
- Austrian truck engineer Steyr Nutzfahrzeuge AG, a unit of Germany's truck maker MAN, wants to supply metal sheet to U.S. Chrysler's production plant in southern Austria.
- Raiffeisen agricultural group says it will only participate in Unilever's plant in eastern Austria if it receives all trade mark rights too.
- Austrian exports accounted for 37.5 percent of GDP, ranking the country seventh within the European Union.
- Tyrolean Airways pre-tax profits jumped 32.2 percent to 104.2 million schillings in 1996.
- Voest Alpine Intertrading doubled its earnings in 1996 and will pay 139 million schillings in dividends.
- Constructor Bau-Holding plans a capital increase in autumn tied to its takeover of Germany's Leonhard Moll AG's construction units.
DIE PRESSE
- Conservatives are pushing for a speedy privatisation of the City of Vienna's stake in Bank Austria.
- A road pricing system is now expected to be only introduced for trucks and not for cars, after protests by the conservative junior coalition partner.

- The federal government and the state governments of Vienna and Lower Austria have signed a syndicate agreement to jointly appoint future chief executives of the listed Vienna airport operator Flughafen Wien.
KURIER

- The opposition Greens say they have documents proving the government informed parliament falsely about its involvement in the affair surrounding the release of the alleged Iranian killers of three Kurdish leaders in 1989.
- Industry plans to create 30,000 new jobs for the unemployed by paying wages under the collective agreement.
WIRTSCHAFTSBLATT
- Heinz Gehl, chief executive of Bank Austria, says Austria's banks have a surplus of 7,000 employees.
- Oil and chemicals group OMV plans to increase competitivity by slimming down its organisational structures.
